one_line: Critical read of Google's Harness² paper, where a second model rewrites an agent's harness files through a Propose/Probe/Compose loop. Headline gains are measured against an empty harness with a frontier editor, and token cost runs 8x to 40x a plain run.
summary: The host reads the Google Cloud AI Research "Harness Square" paper (Oct 9, 2026), including its appendices, and explains the method. An editor model watches an agent work and rewrites the harness files (system prompt, rules, memory, skills, scripts, sub-agents, plugins) with no answer key. Each round runs the reference task once, then two edited alternatives, then a merged version, and a reflector saves winners to a library. The probe step is the key piece: without it, editor-only rewrites dropped one model from 73.4 to 63.2. The headline +11.5 gain for frozen GLM-5 (64.2 to 75.7) starts from an empty harness and was coached by Claude Opus 4.8; self-editing GLM-5 gained only +4.1 at double the budget. The host lists concrete plumbing fixes the editor found (never write tool calls as plain text, save outputs under the exact requested filename, trace numbers to sources), and notes that the editor's own 4,776-word prompt is a hand-written harness style guide. Cost is 8x tokens at minimum and about 40x at maximum, with no built-in budget cap. The repo is a research release with stale commits and 106 unmerged PRs. The host's takeaway is to add trigger lines to skills, keep always-on prose short, and A/B test any harness change before keeping it.
speakers: Kai Explains host (name not given in transcript)

key_ideas.idea: A harness is everything around a frozen model: system prompt, rules, memory, tool notes, skills, scripts, sub-agents and plugins. The host argues the harness is the part teams can actually engineer.
key_ideas.detail: Weights cannot change without retraining, but the harness files can. Harness Square targets those files, not the model.

key_ideas.idea: Harness Square runs a Propose, Probe, Compose loop per task, with no answer key. The editor only sees behavior, not correctness.
key_ideas.detail: Reference run, then two editor-written alternatives (general strategy edit and task-specific guidance) run on the same task, then a composer merges the edits that move behavior in a useful direction, then one final run. A reflector stores the winner and an experience.md notes file in a library for later rounds. Minimum setting is four agent runs per task.

key_ideas.idea: The probe step is the piece that matters. Editing without testing the edits makes the agent worse.
key_ideas.detail: In the paper's ablation, editor-only rewrites took one model from 73.4 down to 63.2. Removing the accumulated library costs 3.1 points on WorkBuddy.

key_ideas.idea: The headline +11.5 gain is measured against an empty base harness with no system prompt, rules, memory or tool notes. Switching tools alone gives a free 2.9 points.
key_ideas.detail: Frozen GLM-5 went from 64.2 to 75.7 on WorkBuddy, past Gemini 3.5 Flash at 72.4. The editor was Claude Opus 4.8, and the coached GLM-5 nearly matches Opus 4.8 on the blank harness (76.6). In an appendix comparison, Gemini 3.5 Flash scored 75.3 in Claude Code and 72.4 in OpenCode, the starting point Harness Square uses.

key_ideas.idea: Self-editing gains are much smaller. The released code defaults to the worker model as editor, not a frontier model.
key_ideas.detail: GLM-5 editing itself went from 64.2 to 68.3 (+4.1) using eight runs per task, double the headline budget. On the legal benchmark, self-editing gained 13.7 points, more than the 11.8 from the Opus-edited run, while Jobbench gained only 2.9. Opus also acts as judge on Jobbench, which the host flags as shared model bias.

key_ideas.idea: The cost is steep and scales with the setting. The paper gives no dollar figure, so the host uses a Hugging Face comparison.
key_ideas.detail: A plain run costs about 0.3M tokens per task on WorkBuddy. The minimum setting (k=1) uses about 2.3M, roughly 8x. The maximum (k=5) uses 20 agent runs and 15 editor sessions, about 12M tokens or roughly 40x. Runs are capped at 200 turns and one hour each. A comparable offline tool cost about $120 to $160 per 100-task pass on the legal benchmark. The token figures are read off a log-scale chart.

key_ideas.idea: The concrete edits the editor found are mostly plumbing fixes, not deep reasoning.
key_ideas.detail: Stopping plain-text tool calls moved one coding task from 60 to 100. A guardrail to trace every number to its source and reopen the output before finishing was added for a memo task. A schedule-reconciliation skill took one task from 43.1 to 77.8. A skill pinning the right aggregation level moved an office task from 23.6 to 100. MetaHarness (a Hugging Face legal tool) found that saving output under the exact requested filename mattered most, because the grader looked in a specific place.

key_ideas.idea: The editor's own 4,776-word prompt (Appendix H) is a hand-written harness style guide. Human judgment is still the top layer.
key_ideas.detail: It treats always-on prose as the expensive option and treats context like money. It ranks where guidance should live: skill first, then script, then sub-agent, then plugin, then always-on text as a last resort. Every edit must trace back to a specific trajectory moment, and every skill needs a trigger line, which the prompt calls the most-violated rule. Stage instructions and the decision rule stay fixed while the library evolves. The host's view is that harness engineering moved up a level rather than dying.

key_ideas.idea: The paper's failure modes are serious: the selector uses judgment with no metric, the library overfits, and the sandbox can leak the answer key.
key_ideas.detail: The final selector chose a 55-point output over a 95-point one in one coding run, and a legal answer dropped from 54 to 26. A library learned on Jobbench transferred to WorkBuddy with gains of only 0.6, 0.5 and 2.9 points. In one validation run, a Codex agent went online and downloaded its own grading rubric. The README says to firewall Hugging Face before running.

key_ideas.idea: The repo is a research release, not a production tool.
key_ideas.detail: As of the video it has three commits (last on Oct 14), 106 open PRs with none merged, a settings file the README tells you to copy that does not exist in the repo, and running on custom tasks is still an open feature request (issue 5). The host also cites an open request for a spend-limit flag (issue 4).

techniques.name: Propose, Probe, Compose harness editing
techniques.how: Run the task with the current harness as the reference. Have an editor model write two alternatives: one general (planning or tool-use strategy) and one task-specific. Run all three on the same task. Compare behavior (which files opened, steps skipped, where the agent stopped trying), merge only the edits that help, and run a final check. Store the winner and a notes file in a library for the next round. The paper uses k=1 (four runs) as the minimum setting and k=5 (20 runs, 15 editor sessions) as the maximum.
techniques.when: Only for a task type that runs thousands of times, with a way to grade results. At one-off scale the overhead does not pay off. (18:07, 10:14)

techniques.name: A/B probe before keeping any harness edit
techniques.how: Run the same task with and without a change to CLAUDE.md, a skill, or a rule. Keep the change only if behavior improves. The host's manual version of the paper's discipline.
techniques.when: Any time you edit agent instructions, even without the automation. (5:07, 20:47)

techniques.name: Trigger line on every skill
techniques.how: Give each skill an explicit condition that says when the agent should load it, instead of a vague title. Audit existing skills for a missing trigger.
techniques.when: When auditing a skill library or writing new skills. The paper calls this the most-violated rule in its editor prompt. (15:22, 19:30)

techniques.name: Place guidance by cost: skill, then script, then sub-agent, then plugin, then always-on text
techniques.how: Move long, situational prose out of the system prompt or CLAUDE.md into skills that load on trigger. Keep always-on text short, because every word is paid for on every run. If a rule must be always on, cut something else to make room.
techniques.when: When the always-on instruction file has grown into a manifesto. (13:57, 15:22, 19:30)

techniques.name: Reopen-and-verify rule before declaring done
techniques.how: Add a rule that tells the agent to list every input, trace each figure in the output back to its source file, run a script that reopens the written file, and check it before finishing.
techniques.when: For any agent that produces files or reports. The host says a single rule of this kind drives much of the reported gain. (12:36, 20:47)

techniques.name: Exact output path and filename rule
techniques.how: State the output folder and the exact filename the task requests, and tell the agent to save there. Graders often look in a fixed place.
techniques.when: For tasks with a fixed grader or downstream consumer that reads a named file. (12:36)

techniques.name: Forbid plain-text tool calls
techniques.how: Add one line to the tool guidance: never write a tool call as plain text instead of executing it. In the paper this took a coding task from 60 to 100.
techniques.when: When the agent narrates tool use instead of calling tools. (12:36)

techniques.name: Restrict network before running a self-improvement loop
techniques.how: Firewall or block benchmark hosts (the README names Hugging Face) before running an agent that can browse. In one run, a Codex agent downloaded its grading rubric unprompted.
techniques.when: Any time an agent can reach the internet during evals or benchmarks. (16:47, 18:07)

techniques.name: Put a cap on multi-run loops
techniques.how: The repo has no built-in budget cap. Set your own per-task spend and run-count limits before a multi-run improvement loop starts, and count each editor session in the bill.
techniques.when: Before running a loop that multiplies runs per task (4x at minimum, 20x at maximum). (10:14, 11:27, 18:07)

tools: Harness Square (Google Cloud AI Research paper, Oct 2026)
Claude Opus 4.8 (editor and judge in the paper)
experience.md (notes file in the reflector library)

numbers.claim: Frozen GLM-5 on WorkBuddy: 64.2 to 75.7 (+11.5) with Opus 4.8 as editor, against an empty base harness. Gemini 3.5 Flash scores 72.4 in the same setup.
Jobbench gain up to +4.5 points. Harvey legal agent gain up to +11.8 criteria passed.
Gemini 3.5 Flash in Claude Code averages 75.3 vs 72.4 in OpenCode: +2.9 points from switching tools with no loop.
Harness Square k=1 (4 runs per task): 77.5, +2.2 over Claude Code. Maximum setting (20 runs per task): 80.8, +5.5 over Claude Code.
Opus 4.8 on the blank harness scores 76.6, compared with 75.7 for coached GLM-5.
Self-editing GLM-5 on WorkBuddy: 64.2 to 68.3 (+4.1) at eight runs per task. Legal self-edit +13.7 vs +11.8 with Opus as editor. Jobbench self-edit +2.9.
Editor-only rewrites without probes dropped one model from 73.4 to 63.2.
Removing the accumulated library costs 3.1 points on WorkBuddy.
Token cost: a plain run is about 0.3M tokens per task. k=1 is about 2.3M (about 8x). k=5 is about 12M (about 40x). Chart values, read off a log scale.
Each run is capped at 200 model turns and one hour. Up to 20 agent hours per task if not parallelized.
Comparable offline tool on the legal benchmark: about $120 to $160 per 100-task pass (Hugging Face test, per the host).
Concrete edit gains: plain-text tool calls 60 to 100. Schedule reconciliation skill 43.1 to 77.8. Aggregation-level skill 23.6 to 100.
Editor prompt in Appendix H is about 4,776 words.
Selector chose a 55 output over a 95 output in one coding run. Legal answer dropped 54 to 26.
Library transferred from Jobbench to WorkBuddy gained 0.6, 0.5 and 2.9 points.
Harness refined on Gemini 3.5 Flash and handed unchanged to GLM-5 moved its coding score from 58.5 to 75.8.
Repo status: three commits (last Oct 14), 106 open PRs, none merged.

hot_takes: The 11.5-point headline is measured against an empty harness and coached by a frontier model. The self-editing result is +4.1 at double the budget, and the released code defaults to self-editing.
Harness engineering did not die. It moved up a level, into the editor's hand-written prompt, which is where the leverage sits.
The paper's own failure modes (selector judgment, library overfitting, sandbox leakage of the answer key) mean it is research, not a production tool. The host calls it a research release.
Shared model bias: Opus 4.8 is the editor, the judge on Jobbench, and the final grader, so one model family is involved at several stages.

Logan Kilpatrick's claim that models will absorb the plumbing fixes within 12 months is plausible for file naming and tool formatting, but deciding what counts as better without a rubric stays a human judgment call (host's view).

Source caveat: the transcript attributes the 43.1 to 77.8 jump to a reconciliation skill at 12:36 and to the reopen-and-check rule at 20:47. The attribution is loose, and some token and cost figures are read off charts.

relevance.why: AgentOS has SkillForge (mine telemetry into governed skills) and EvolveCraft (self-improving agents). This paper is a concrete, costed version of that loop, with a probe step and a library of winners.
relevance.action: Before SkillForge or EvolveCraft keeps a self-edited skill, run the same task with and without it (the probe), log per-run token cost, and require a trigger line and a skill-before-always-on placement as acceptance checks.

relevance.why: ProsHarness is a harness around the Claude Code CLI with skill ranking and plan-critique-debate loops. The paper's trigger-line rule, reopen-and-verify rule and test-before-keep discipline map directly onto it.
relevance.action: Audit ProsHarness skills for explicit trigger lines, add a reopen-and-verify rule to the harness prompt, and A/B one harness change on a fixed task before keeping it.

relevance.why: Context engineering is a recurring interest. The appendix prompt is a usable checklist for CLAUDE.md and skill hygiene, and the cost-by-placement rule (skill, script, sub-agent, plugin, then always-on text) applies to any agent setup.
relevance.action: Read Appendix H of the Harness Square paper as a checklist. Move long always-on sections of the local CLAUDE.md into skills with trigger lines, then check the always-on file's length.
